call_targets.note: M223 called these 19 call targets 'functions' with bodies capped at the next root. That cap is what produced the 216 'gap' words; the targets that share an exit are entry points into one body, and the ones whose head is a bare `jr` are calls that only run their delay slot. The word 'function' is retracted for the count.

sp_not_programmed.quote: With the current software architecture, the application does not program the SP directly, and need not concern itself with IMEM and DMEM accesses.

link_saves.reading: the four `or fp,zero,ra` instructions in this program are at ['0x2c8', '0x3d8', '0x87c', '0xcac'] and none of them is reachable, while 3 `jr fp` exits are. So on every path this model can find, the body returns through a register that no instruction writes: either the program's call displacements do not line up with its code (a patched or relinked blob), or the entry register state carries fp — and the manual says nothing about the RSP's register state at task start (M223 E3b). Recorded as the standing doubt about the call layout, not resolved.

returns.note: `jr` with a register other than ra/fp is still a return when the register provably holds a saved link; each such site is listed with the instruction that saved it

control_flow.rule: Successors are per instruction, with the delay slot modelled as its own step: a `j`/`jal`/`jr` at a has a -> a+4 only, and the delay slot at a+4 then has the jump's target (or, for `jr`, the return set). A branch at a has a -> a+4, and its delay slot has {taken, a+8}. `break` has no successor. `beq zero,zero,T` is read as an unconditional jump and `bne zero,zero,T` as never taken: the assembler emits that pair when a branch is out of range, and treating it as conditional both invents an edge into whatever follows and hides the one to T. The return set for `jr ra`/`jr fp` is every `jal` return address (site+8) plus every synthesized return (`ori ra,zero,imm`): an over-approximation, and it is why a word this tool calls unreachable is unreachable under *more* edges than the hardware has, not fewer.

cpu_side.note: The CPU computes a flush length of count x stride with a shift/add chain and never stores the stride. Feeding one unit through the exact instructions gives 2576 = 0xa10, which is the same constant the RSP advances its record pointer by at 0x27c.

cpu_contract.reading: The CPU publishes a pointer (task +0x30) and a count (+0x34), flushes count x 0xa10 bytes of it, and the RSP reads both once, walks records of 0xa10 bytes and decrements the count. That is a record walk, not a command list: nothing in the record selects which code runs, and the only CPU-published value that reaches a branch is the count.

evidence: the program has 49 `jal`/`j` instructions and every one carries an absolute IMEM target: there is no computed transfer to dispatch through
no load anywhere in the program is used as a jump or call target: the only indirect transfers are `jr` through a saved link (listed under control_flow.returns)
13 loads feed a conditional branch within 8 instructions; they are the fields that select stages of the frame loop, and none of them indexes a target
the fields are sizes, counts and mode flags: they are added into buffer arithmetic, shifted, masked with small constants, or zero-tested to skip a stage
dispatch.reading: The CPU-published block is a parameter record the ucode branches on, not a command stream it dispatches on. That is the same shape M220 measured on the sound side: the 'macros' were a class tag, and here the 'commands' are record fields.
dispatch.verdict: no command dispatch — measured, not asserted

dmem_map.rule: A base register qualifies only if every write to it in the program is a constant form (`ori`/`addiu`/`lui`, or a move from a register that itself qualifies). Then the absolute address is that constant plus the instruction's 16-bit displacement. A register with one unfoldable write is disqualified, so nothing here is guessed.

cross_checks: the length values this program writes are all n-1 for a multiple of 8, which is what the cited rule predicts and M223 could not check: every length stated as an immediate is bytes-1 with bytes a multiple of 8 (see register_primitives.lengths_summary)

the entry's first instruction reads COP0 register 11, which is *outside* the cited set c0-c7 — so the register M223 called "the RSP status register, name from outside authority" is not the documented status register (c4), and this program never reads c4
the one write to c4 sets bit 14 and is followed by `break`: on a write that bit is SET_SIG2 (cited), so the halt path raises signal 2 and stops

external_sources.why: The local Programming Manual settles the RSP's structure but not its registers: p115 says the application does not program the SP directly, and the index lists the header it defers device bit patterns to (`rcp.h`) against pages 110-111 only, which are the DP, VI, AI and PI status registers. So the register map comes from outside this repository, and it is labelled as external wherever it is used. Facts only — numbers, names and stated behaviour. No text is reproduced and no code is taken.

argument_order.reading: Two of the four transfer entries write c0 from a1 and c1 from a2; the other two write c0 from a2 and c1 from a1. Every value either side takes is below 0x1000 — the program's RDRAM addresses span 0x000 to 0xd60 and its DMEM addresses 0x000 to 0xfff — so the two address spaces are indistinguishable by value, and the register assignment is the only thing that says which side is which. That makes the pair of calls at 0x00dc and 0x00e4 the sharpest open question here: they pass the *same two values* to entries that assign them to c0/c1 in opposite orders.

lengths_summary.note: the cited rule says a length register holds bytes-1 and every transfer size is a multiple of 8. Every length this program states as an immediate obeys it; the computed ones are listed with their fold rather than counted, and the count of folded sites is asserted below so this cannot pass on an empty set.

register_primitives.register_map: cited: N64brew Wiki, Reality_Signal_Processor/Interface, revision 5376 (CC BY-SA-4.0), for the COP0 numbers and the write-triggers-a-transfer behaviour. The local Programming Manual does not map them — p115 says the application does not program the SP directly and its index lists rcp.h only against pp110-111 (DP/VI/AI/PI status) — so this is an external source, recorded as one.

semaphore_protocol.reading: a read of c7 returns the old bit and leaves it set (cited), so `mfc0` followed by `bne ...,zero,<back>` spins until the mutex is free and acquires it; `mtc0 zero` releases it. Every transfer entry takes the mutex around its DMA except the one that writes only RAMADDR and the length.

status_bit_14.measurement: the only write to c4 stores 0x4000 from an immediate, and the next two instructions are `nop` then `break`.
status_bit_14.reading: on a write, SP_STATUS bit 14 is SET_SIG2 (cited), so the halt path raises signal bit 2 and stops the RSP. The CPU side of that handshake is the handler installed at *0x80143ff0, which is not in this image: stage-2 contains zero references to 0xa4040010.

rsp_only.why: M225 named 252 of them from a cited table and left 2 refused, so the *instructions* are known here; what they compute for the mixer is not. A name says which opcode runs, not which signal path it serves, and the structure is in the accumulator's use across the frame loop, which no document describes

rsp_only.why: the register numbers written are measured ([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7]) and named from the cited map, and the values at every call site are folded — but which of the two address fields is the DMEM side is decided by the register assignment alone, because every value either side takes is under 0x1000 (see argument_order)

rsp_only.cpu_evidence: none — the CPU never writes IMEM after the task starts

rsp_only.why: they are code (branches, calls and returns inside them) and nothing enters them under an edge set that is strictly larger than the hardware's. Whether they are dead, or reached by a mechanism outside this model, is not decided here

vector_transfers.rule: the row is in bits 15:11, the element in 10:7 and the offset in 6:0, and the address is base + offset * access_size (cited). The split and the row names are taken from tools/rsp_decode.py, which owns that decode; this tool folds the base register and nothing else. M223 read bits 15:0 as a 16-bit signed displacement and excluded all of these accesses, which is retracted.
